editorial.headline: Sound Recording: Open Nationally, Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Sound-recording work is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium means a foreign investor cannot register it on the island today.
editorial.body:
At its core, this is the business of making sound permanent and usable. It includes the creation of original master sound recordings, recording services, and the production of pre-recorded radio programmes rather than live broadcasts. Its territory also reaches audio podcasts, sound made for film, television, books and other media, and the conversion of recorded material into audio-streaming formats. The listed examples prevent the activity from being reduced to music alone: spoken programmes and media-bound audio are expressly within its field. Nor is it confined to capture at the microphone; converting recordings for audio streaming is also part of the defined work.

This can be a very small operation or a large one. Registration is open across the Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales, so the category does not reserve sound-recording work for a single type of studio or producer. A compact specialist setup can sit within the same formal activity as a larger production operation, provided the work remains within the defined field: original masters, recording services, pre-recorded audio programming, audio for media, and conversion to streaming format. The stated scale range makes room for the same activity to be carried out at distinctly different commercial sizes.

The national position is clear. The PMA status is TERBUKA, with a national foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In national terms, foreign investment is open up to full ownership. A 100% national foreign-ownership ceiling does not override Bali’s island-wide PMA restriction. That distinction matters because a national entry position and a provincial registration outcome can point in different directions.

For Bali, the outcome today is direct: a foreign investor cannot register this activity for PMA. At the Besar scale, its OSS risk is Low or Medium-Low across every scope, which places it within Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium on PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities. The moratorium dates from May 2026. This block is tied to the recorded risk position at the Besar scale, not to any reduction in the national ownership ceiling. Nationally, the activity remains open to full foreign ownership; in Bali, its present PMA registration position is blocked.
editorial.pullQuote: A 100% national foreign-ownership ceiling does not override Bali’s island-wide PMA restriction.
